document.title: Afghanistan: In July 2 Meeting, [Excised] Defends Discriminatory Edicts on Women and Girls, and Controls on NGO's
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Taliban File Update
document.note: [Confidential] Embassy official Joe Novak meets a source who appears to be Taliban official Abdul Mujahid, urging withdrawal of edicts discriminating against women and controlling NGOs. Mujahid confirms the GOP 300 million rupee commitment and smiles when told it pays Taliban salaries. He says the Taliban keep tight control of bin Laden and that forcing him out is implausible given Mullah Omar's commitment to him.

events.description: Acting Political Counselor met Taliban representative in Islamabad, urging withdrawal of edicts on girls' schools, women's medical care, and NGO relocation.
Bin Ladin in Khost gave press statements threatening the U.S. (May-early June).
Saudi intelligence chief Prince Turki recently visited Kandahar to press Taliban on Bin Ladin.
Pakistan committed 300 million rupees (USD 6 million) to the Taliban, not yet delivered.

Meeting at which an excised Taliban interlocutor defended discriminatory edicts on women and girls and NGO controls. He showed little sign of backing down and said he would pass U.S. views to Kabul and Kandahar.
Embassy reports the Taliban are considering replacing an official with Sher Mohammad Stanakzai.
US Acting Political Counselor met a Taliban representative, urging withdrawal of edicts on girls' schools, women's medical treatment and NGO relocation.
Pakistan agreed to provide the Taliban 300 million rupees (USD 6 million); not yet delivered as of July 2.
Bin Ladin issued press statements threatening the US while in Khost Province, May to early June 1998.
Prince Turki recently visited Kandahar to press the Taliban on bin Ladin.
The Taliban imposed new controls on bin Ladin in Kandahar, requiring clearance of his activities and interviews.
Pakistan/Iran peace team sent to Mazar-i-Sharif and Kandahar; may already have visited Kandahar.

key_claims: Taliban interlocutor defended edicts closing home-based girls' schools, restricting women's hospital access, and relocating NGOs to a single compound.
Pakistan admitted to committing 300 million rupees to the Taliban, which the US suspected was for salaries of officials and commanders.
The Taliban claimed Bin Ladin was 'under control' in Kandahar and must clear all activities and press interviews with them.
Saudi intelligence chief Prince Turki visited Kandahar pressing the Taliban on Bin Ladin, but Mullah Omar would not turn against him.
The Taliban regarded the Pakistan/Iran peace effort as a non-starter because they distrust Iran.
The Taliban considered replacing New York representative Abdul Wahab with Sher Mohammad Stanakzai.
The US acknowledged very little influence over Kabul and Kandahar.
